newsitem.title: UK: Strikebound BA seeks union talks.
newsitem.headline: Strikebound BA seeks union talks.

text.p: British Airways on Thursday called on striking flight attendants to reopen talks over pay and a plan to save $70.8 million as the two-day-old disruption continued to ground flights and strand thousands of passengers.

The airline expected disruption from the planned 72-hour strike to spill over into the weekend before operations returned to normal, with only 75 percent of its usual long-haul flights likely to operate Saturday.
On Wednesday, the airline was forced to cancel 20 percent to 30 percent of the 1,000 flights it operates worldwide each day, leaving 25,000 passengers stranded.
There was no contact between the management and unions Thursday, effectively ending hopes that the strike could be called off before Friday.

The industrial action is part of a war British Airways is fighting on several fronts. The carrier is striving to get clearance for a massive alliance with American Airlines, while also fighting off a legal challenge from Laker Airway Inc. in Florida.

Mike Street, the airline's director of operations, told a news conference he was urging the British Airways Stewards and Stewardesses Association (BASSA) to hold fresh talks with management over a pay deal that a breakaway cabin crew union has already accepted.

"We have an opportunity now to sort out the strike with BASSA. We have to have a better relationship. ... We're ready at any time to sit down and talk, but we won't unpick (undo) a deal we've discussed (with unions) over five months," Street said.

The strike is being held over a new pay structure the airline has put into effect as part of a massive cost-saving drive, in which it hopes to slash 42 million pounds ($70.8 million) from its operating budget

The airline has threatened to take legal action against the strikers. BA claims the 72-hour strike, which is set to continue until Saturday morning, is illegal because of a discrepancy in the strike ballot. The airline says more cabin crew members voted on the strike ballot than were actually on the company payroll.
Management has warned that employees face loss of travel perks and opportunities of promotion if they went on strike, and threatened to fire or even sue individual strikers.
BA also recruited staff replacements, chartered seven aircraft and offered flight attendants taxis and hotel accommodations to ensure that staff turned up for work Friday, it said.
George Ryde, the Transport & General Workers Union's senior official, said chartering aircraft would make little difference to the impact of the strike, which he said received "solid support."

BA, meanwhile, said some 1,600 staff members had come into work Thursday while only 250 had gone on strike. But a further 1,700 have so far called to say they would not be coming in for work, rather than admit they were striking for fear of reprisals from the airline.
BA's Street estimated the strike had already cost the carrier "considerably more than the pilots' dispute last year, which didn't even become a strike."
The pilots' dispute is estimated to have cost BA 15 million pounds ($25.3 million).
